newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-West Australia miners fear new royalty tax on gold.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-West Australia miners fear new royalty tax on gold.

text.p: A gold royalty plan being considered by the Western Australia government threatens to make some mining operations in Australia's leading gold mining state uneconomic if it is implemented, mining executives said on Wednesday.
Facing a potential loss of around A$33 million in federal funds this year, the state is looking at ways to lift revenues, including imposing a royalty on gold.
Western Australia produces about 70 percent of Australia's nearly 300 tonnes of gold each year and a gold royalty is seen adding tens of millions of dollars in revenues to the state.
Unlike in other states, gold miners in Western Australia currently are exempt from paying any royalties on gold.

Queensland has a 2.75-percent gross royalty, while in New South Wales a net smelter levy of four percent is equal to about a two-percent gross royalty. The Northern Territory has an 18-percent net profit royalty.
Advocates of the royalty claim is unfair that Western Australia is exempt, given the enormity of the gold sector.
But opponents maintain that the lack of a royalty enable miners to sometimes work otherwise low-grade and uneconomic deposits since they can retain the full value of the gold
"It helps to allow us to mine lower grade deposits," Les Emery, managing director of Lynas Gold.
"No one (miners) want the imposition of further costs," Collis Thorpe, managing director of Consolidated Gold NL said.
"Marginal producers could face real problems if they are hit with additional costs," Thorpe added.

State Premier Richard Court is expected to fuel debate over a royalty at the start of the annual Australian Gold Conference on Wednesday in the mining town of Kalgoorlie, where he was scheduled to speak.

Court has not ruled out a royalty, although he has said in the past one alternative might be to exempt smaller mining companies and explorers from any programme. This would leave big mining companies pay the levy.
However, exploration might still feel the effects since most small companies rely on larger ones for funding and farm in arrangements, Emery said.
"Indirectly, it would still hurt," Emery said.
Western Australia Resources Minister Colin Barnett has come out in support of a tax and the idea is winning favour among other sectors of government.

There also is a mounting public perception that gold miners are not shouldering their fair share, an issue disputed by miners, who claim they already pay high taxes, create jobs and fuel economic growth.

Consolidated Gold's Thorpe said the problem was exacerbated by current weak gold prices. He said a royalty has the potential to encourage more mining and exploration companies to abandon Australia and look overseas for new mines.
"Australia is not the only place with gold," Thorpe said.
Stockbroker ANZ Securities estimates that a two-percent royalty, would cause the market-weighted average of companies affected to decline 3.6 percent.
The average decline is valuation for the Australian gold sector as a whole would be 2.3 percent, ANZ said in a recent report.
Western Australia produces about 70 percent of Australia's gold each year, figures from the Association of Mining and Exploration Companies (Inc) of Western Australia show.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
